whole Walsh tree, of which this family is the largest modern branch: Mike Shanahan was Seifert's coordinator
in San Francisco before he went to Denver. This section zooms in on the part of it that calls plays today.

The family has two roots in the Denver building of the 1990s. Gary Kubiak, Mike Shanahan's coordinator, carried
the system to Houston as head coach (2006–13) and back to Denver, where he won Super Bowl 50 after the 2015
season; his sons Klint and Klay are coaches in it now. Kyle Shanahan took it through Houston, Washington,
Cleveland and Atlanta to San Francisco. The decisive moment was the Washington staff of 2010–13, under Mike
Shanahan with Kyle as offensive coordinator: Sean McVay coached the tight ends, Matt LaFleur the quarterbacks,
and Mike McDaniel (from 2011) was an offensive assistant and then the receivers coach. All four became NFL head coaches.[^was] (That Washington offense
also produced one of the scheme's purest seasons: in 2012 Alfred Morris, a sixth-round rookie, ran for 1,613
yards in wide zone, beside rookie quarterback Robert Griffin III and the read-option plays the staff borrowed
from Baylor, which [The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd) covers.)[^morris]

From there it branched. McVay's own staffs in Los Angeles produced head coaches Zac Taylor (Bengals, 2019),
Kevin O'Connell (Vikings, 2022) and Liam Coen (Jaguars, 2025). LaFleur took the system to Green Bay in 2019;
Aaron Rodgers won two MVPs in it. Kyle's 49ers staffs produced McDaniel (Dolphins, 2022), Mike LaFleur (Matt's
brother) and Brian Fleury, and they gave Klint Kubiak a season on the staff before he went on to run offenses in
New Orleans and Seattle.

Staffs change every winter, and this one changed a lot. @fig-staff-moves lays out who held which job in the
2025 season and the 2026 season.

```{python}
#| label: fig-staff-moves
#| fig-cap: "Recent staff moves: the Shanahan family's play-callers and coordinators, 2025 season vs 2026 season (staffs as of October 2026). Each row is one coach; the left card is his 2025 job, the right card his 2026 job. Orange cards changed over the winter. 'Calls plays' marks the coach who called his offense's plays that season; in 2026 it is left off where the team had not confirmed who calls them. The family lost a head coach in Miami and gained two, in Las Vegas and Arizona; Seattle replaced one family play-caller with another."
# (coach, how he joined the family, 2025 job, 2026 job, calls plays 2025, calls plays 2026)
MOVES = [
    ("Kyle Shanahan", "Mike Shanahan's son; Kubiak's Texans", "49ers head coach", "49ers head coach", True, True),
    ("Sean McVay", "Washington staff 2010–16", "Rams head coach", "Rams head coach", True, True),
    ("Matt LaFleur", "Washington, Atlanta; McVay's OC 2017", "Packers head coach", "Packers head coach", True, True),
    ("Mike McDaniel", "Kyle's staffs, Houston to SF", "Dolphins head coach", "Chargers offensive coordinator", True, False),
    ("Klint Kubiak", "Gary Kubiak's son; 49ers staff", "Seahawks offensive coordinator", "Raiders head coach", True, False),
    # 2026 play-calling for Kubiak (LV), Mike LaFleur (ARI) and McDaniel (LAC) is left unmarked: not confirmed
    ("Mike LaFleur", "Kyle's staffs; Matt's brother", "Rams offensive coordinator", "Cardinals head coach", False, False),
    ("Brian Fleury", "49ers staff 2019–25", "49ers run-game coord. & TEs", "Seahawks offensive coordinator", False, True),
    ("Klay Kubiak", "Gary Kubiak's son; 49ers staff", "49ers offensive coordinator", "49ers offensive coordinator", False, False),
    ("Kevin O'Connell", "McVay's OC 2020–21", "Vikings head coach", "Vikings head coach", True, True),
    ("Liam Coen", "McVay's Rams staffs", "Jaguars head coach", "Jaguars head coach", True, True),
    ("Zac Taylor", "McVay's Rams 2017–18", "Bengals head coach", "Bengals head coach", True, True),
]
W, H = 6.6, 0.34 * len(MOVES) + 0.75
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(W, H))
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
ax.set_xlim(0, W); ax.set_ylim(0, H); ax.axis("off")
X_NAME, X25, X26, CW, CH = 0.06, 1.84, 4.26, 2.28, 0.27
ax.text(X25 + CW / 2, H - 0.2, "2025 season", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold",
        color=style.INK)
ax.text(X26 + CW / 2, H - 0.2, "2026 season", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold",
        color=style.INK)
ax.text(X_NAME, H - 0.2, "Coach (how he joined the family)", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=7.6,
        fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2)
for i, (name, root, j25, j26, c25, c26) in enumerate(MOVES):
    y = H - 0.55 - i * 0.34
    changed = j25 != j26
    ax.text(X_NAME, y + 0.055, name, fontsize=7.4, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center")
    ax.text(X_NAME, y - 0.085, root, fontsize=5.8, color=style.INK_2, va="center")
    for xc, job, calls, hot in [(X25, j25, c25, False), (X26, j26, c26, changed)]:
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((xc, y - CH / 2), CW, CH, boxstyle="round,pad=0.01,rounding_size=0.05",
                                    fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT if hot else style.SURFACE,
                                    ec=style.DEFENSE if hot else style.BASELINE, lw=1.1 if hot else 0.7))
        ax.text(xc + 0.07, y, job, fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, va="center",
                fontweight="bold" if hot else "normal")
        if calls:
            ax.text(xc + CW - 0.07, y, "calls plays", fontsize=5.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="center",
                    ha="right", style="italic")
    ax.annotate("", (X26 - 0.03, y), xytext=(X25 + CW + 0.03, y),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.DEFENSE if changed else style.BASELINE, lw=0.9))
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-staff-moves with the season labels in mind, because the two lists are easy to blur.

**In the 2025 season** the family's play-callers ran the 49ers (Kyle Shanahan), the Rams (McVay, with Mike
LaFleur as offensive coordinator), the Packers (Matt LaFleur), the Dolphins (McDaniel), the Seahawks (Klint
Kubiak, as offensive coordinator under defensive head coach Mike Macdonald), and, a generation down, the
Vikings, Jaguars and Bengals. The season ended with the family everywhere: the NFC Championship Game was Seattle
against the Rams, 31–27, and Seattle went on to win Super Bowl LX 29–13 over New England.[^lx]

**In the 2026 season** the map is different. Miami fired McDaniel in January and he became the Chargers'
offensive coordinator; Klint Kubiak became the Raiders' head coach after his one season in Seattle; Mike
LaFleur left the Rams to become the Cardinals' head coach; Seattle replaced Kubiak with Brian Fleury, the 49ers'
run-game coordinator and tight ends coach, so the Seahawks stayed in the family. In San Francisco, Shanahan still calls the plays with
Klay Kubiak as offensive coordinator, and in Los Angeles Nathan Scheelhaase was promoted to replace Mike
LaFleur.[^staffs]

The lesson of the moves board is how the system *spreads*: not by teams copying film, but by assistants
leaving with the playbook and the vocabulary in their heads. That is also why the family's offenses differ. A
coordinator who leaves takes the ideas, but he builds them around his own quarterback, his own roster and his
own instincts, which is how a shotgun team in Cincinnati and an under-center team in Los Angeles can share a
grandfather.

## How defenses answered

A system this successful for this long gets studied by every defensive staff in the league. Their answers
fall into four groups, and you will see all four on any Sunday.

**1. Change the front.** The bear in @fig-bear-wide-zone is the oldest answer: cover the interior linemen
so nobody can climb. Its cousin is the [tite front](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd)
(a nose and two linemen on the tackles' inside shoulders), which walls off the middle and asks the edges to
win; and its opposite is a *wide* four-man front with a quick 3-technique who penetrates before the guard's reach
can land ([05-01](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd) animates it).
[Odd and Hybrid Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd) explains why no
single front stops both zone runs, so defenses change fronts by opponent and by down. The offense's counter is
everything in this chapter: the fullback, the unblocked backside end and the boot, and gap runs (counter, duo) out
of the same looks when the front is built for zone.

**2. Keep two safeties deep and play the run with fewer men.** The most important defensive trend of the
2020s, the [two-high](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) shell, is partly an
answer to this family. Play-action and bootlegs work best against a defense that brings a safety down to stop
the run, so defenses led by Vic Fangio and his descendants kept both safeties deep, accepted a
[light box](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd), and trusted bigger fronts
to hold up against the run. Two-high coverage rose from 32.9% of snaps in 2018 to 42.0% in 2025 by Next Gen
Stats' count, the highest since tracking began.[^twohigh] The fight between that idea and this one is the subject
of [Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd), and of
[The Modern Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd).

**3. Take away the middle and make the quarterback hold the ball.** The crossing routes that produce all that
YAC run through the middle of the field at linebacker depth. Fill that area with defenders, rush with
stunts that take a moment to develop, and the quarterback who wanted to throw to a receiver on the move is
holding the ball. The most famous example is New England's plan in Super Bowl LIII, which held McVay's Rams to 3
points; [The Belichick case study](12-02-belichick-patriots-game-plan.qmd) draws it.

**4. Hunt the tells.** An offense built on looking the same can be beaten if it *doesn't* quite look the same.
Defensive staffs grade the running back's depth, the fullback's alignment, the receivers' splits and the
direction of the motion, looking for any detail that separates the run from the boot. That is the self-scouting
war of [08-02](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd): the offense's job is to keep
its tendencies balanced inside each look, and the defense's job is to find the one look that isn't.

And the system answered back. When defenses went light and two-high, the family ran the ball more and got
heavier (in 2025 offenses used fewer than three wide receivers on 41.7% of plays, the highest rate in the Next
Gen Stats era), and when the bear came, the boots came with it.[^heavy] When defenses took away the
crossers, McVay went and got a quarterback who could beat them from the pocket.

## What survives

Ideas from this family are now just *how offense is played* in much of the NFL, including by teams with no
connection to it:

- **Under center is back.** After a decade of shotgun growth, quarterbacks lined up under center more often
  in 2025 than in 2023, led by this family.
- **Motion is universal.** PFF counted a shift or motion on 63.9% of plays in 2025, up from 38.4% in 2016;
  every team but one used it on at least half its plays.[^pff]
- **Heavier personnel is back,** for the same reason the 49ers kept a fullback: to make light defenses pay.
- **YAC as a design goal.** Receivers are now scouted and drafted for what they do after the catch, and
  offenses design throws to catch them on the move.
- **The illusion of complexity** (few plays, many looks; many plays, one look) is standard teaching on almost
  every offensive staff, inside the tree and out.

What may not survive is the specific balance. The 2025 Rams leaned harder on play-action from under center
than anyone, while the 49ers' play-action rate was ordinary, and the second generation in Cincinnati and Atlanta
looks more like a spread offense than like Denver in 1998. A tree spreads by mutating. That is also how you will
know it is still alive: the family resemblance will be in the questions the offense asks a defense, not in any
one formation.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**On Sunday: same look, different plays.** Pick one Shanahan-family offense (in 2026: the 49ers, Rams,
Packers, Vikings, Jaguars, Bengals, Seahawks under Fleury, the Raiders under Klint Kubiak or the Cardinals under
Mike LaFleur) and keep a simple chart for one half.

*Before each snap*

- Write the **look**: personnel (count the backs and tight ends), where the quarterback is (under center or
  shotgun), and the **motion** (none, across, jet, orbit). For example, "21, under center, Z across."
- Is there a **fullback**? If so, where is he: offset to the tight end or away from it?

*In the first second*

- Do all five linemen step the same way? (Zone.) Does the back run toward the tight end? (Wide zone, or a fake of it.)
- Find the **backside end** and watch him. Does he chase the back, or stay home?

*After the play*

- Write what the play turned out to be: wide zone, gap run, bootleg, keeper, play-action shot, dropback.
- If it was a pass, where was the receiver when he caught it: **moving or standing**, and with how much space
  ahead? That is YAC by design.

*At halftime*

- For each look, list the different plays run from it. A good Shanahan-family half has several plays from each
  look; a look that produced only one play is a tendency the defense can find (and so can you). When a look has
  produced a run or two and the backside end has been chasing, start watching for the bootleg from that look.

A template:

| Look (personnel, alignment, motion) | Plays seen | Backside end |
|---|---|---|
| 21, under center, Z across | wide zone R, wide zone R, boot L | chased twice |
| 11, gun, jet from left | jet sweep, play-action cross | stayed home |
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1.** First-and-10 from your own 35, third quarter. The offense is in 21 personnel, the quarterback under
center, the fullback offset to the tight end, who is lined up on the **left** this time. The defense shows the bear
again: the center and both guards covered, eight in the box, one deep safety. On the offense's last three wide-zone
runs toward the tight end, the backside end (on the **right**, ringed) crashed hard down the line after the back,
and one of those runs lost two yards anyway. What is the offense's best call, and which way will it go?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: 21 personnel, offset I, the tight end on the left; a bear front with the strong safety in the box and one deep safety. The backside end (ringed) is on the offense's right."
p = Play(off21(strength="left"), bear(s=-1), los=35, to_go=10)
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-13.5, 13.5), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A bootleg to the right (the side away from the tight end), probably naked, with the keeper built in.** Wide zone
here goes left, toward the tight end, so the play's backside is the offense's right, where the end has been
crashing. Three runs have taught him to chase, and he is the defender the offense leaves unblocked against the
bear. The quarterback fakes wide zone left, keeps the ball and rolls right behind him: the fullback slices into
the right flat, the tight end crosses from left to right behind the linebackers who flowed with the fake, and if
nobody comes up to stop him, the quarterback runs. First-and-10 is the ideal down for it: the defense expects run,
and a short completion keeps the offense on schedule.

*Why not run wide zone again?* Against the bear it was losing yards; the defense has the numbers. The offense's
answer is not to block the bear better but to punish the habit the bear's backside end has fallen into.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2.** Second-and-6, early in the first quarter. The offense has one back and one tight end (11
personnel), the tight end in-line on the left, the quarterback under center and the receivers in tight splits.
Before the snap the Z, a slot receiver on the right, goes in jet motion from right to left (dashed). The defense keeps **two** deep safeties and nobody runs across with the
motion; there are six defenders in the box. Run or pass, and which way?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: 11 personnel under center, the Y in-line on the left, receivers in tight splits; the Z, a slot receiver on the right, goes in jet motion to the left (the dashed arrow ends where he will be at the snap, just behind the quarterback). The defense: a four-man front (a 9 outside the Y, a 3, a 1 and a 5) and two linebackers in the box, a nickel back (NB) who stays outside where the Z started, two cornerbacks and two deep safeties. Nobody follows the motion."
off = named_line(offense("singleback"))
SPOTS = {"Y": (-0.7, -4.8), "H": (-1.5, -10.0), "X": (-0.7, 10.5), "Z": (-1.5, 7.2)}   # Y on the left
off = [q.moved(d=SPOTS[q.key][0], w=SPOTS[q.key][1]) if q.key in SPOTS else
       (q.moved(label="R") if q.key == "RB" else q) for q in off]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.7, "9"), D("LT3", "DT", 1.0, -technique("3"), "3"),
       D("RT1", "DT", 1.0, technique("1"), "1"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5"), "5"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, -1.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, 2.4, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.5, 7.8, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -10.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 10.5, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -6.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 6.5, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=6)
p.motion("Z", to=(-2.6, 1.6))
f = draw(p, lateral=(-14.0, 14.0), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A run: wide zone to the left, toward the tight end and the motion (or the jet sweep itself, handed to the Z).**
Count the box: six defenders against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end), with both safeties 12 yards
deep. That is a [light box](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd), and the system's
standing answer to two-high safeties is to run the ball at them. The motion told the quarterback two more things:
nobody ran across with the Z, so the coverage is very likely zone, and the safeties didn't rotate down, so the box
is staying light. Running toward the motion puts the Z's block (or the threat of the jet sweep, which freezes the
edge defender) on the play side.

*If the defense had answered the motion by walking a safety into the box,* the picture would flip: seven in the box
and one deep safety is the look the play-action shot and the boot are built for.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3.** First-and-10, a series after the bootleg in Drill 1 went for 22 yards. Same 21-personnel look,
tight end on the left, and the defense is in its bear again. But now the backside end on the right has changed:
at the snap of the last wide-zone run he squeezed down the line slowly and stayed square, watching the quarterback,
instead of chasing the back. The defense has stopped the boot. What should the offense call, and if it wants to
boot again, what has to change?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: the same 21-personnel look against the same bear front. The backside end (ringed) is now playing the quarterback, not the back."
p = Play(off21(strength="left"), bear(s=-1), los=35, to_go=10)
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-13.5, 13.5), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
say(f, p, 3.4, 8.6, "squeezes slowly,\neyes on the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Wide zone left again, and if they boot, a protected boot with the fullback assigned to the end.** An end who
stays home to wait for the quarterback is an end who isn't chasing the run. The offense left him unblocked so that
he would have to chase the back from behind; now he has taken himself out of the pursuit altogether, so wide zone is
effectively a play with one fewer defender against it than before. The constraint (the boot) has done its job: it
changed the defense's behaviour, and the base play gets better.

If the offense wants the boot anyway, it can't be naked. The fullback, instead of slicing to the flat, slices across
and *blocks* the end, giving the quarterback time to throw (the protected boot of
[04-05](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)). The cost is one fewer receiver in the flat.
This back-and-forth, base play, constraint, base play, is [sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd),
and it is how a Shanahan play-caller spends a game.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Two problems, one family.** Gibbs's and Mike Shanahan's 1990s Broncos built wide zone and the bootleg to block
  defenses that never stood still; Kyle Shanahan's 2017 49ers added the fullback, motion and YAC passing to beat
  fast, light defenses without a star quarterback.
- **Four ingredients, one picture.** Wide zone moves the defense sideways, the fullback forces a personnel choice,
  motion makes the defense answer first, and YAC passes throw into the space all of that empties. The same few
  looks carry all of it, which is the illusion of complexity.
- **Leave a man free on purpose, then punish him.** Against a bear front the offense can't block everyone, so it
  leaves the backside end and beats him with the bootleg-keeper when he chases. The defense's answer to the base
  play sets up the constraint play.
- **The system raises the quarterback's floor.** Several quarterbacks were much more efficient inside the family
  than outside it, but Goff's Detroit years and the 2021 Stafford trade show the limit: the system can't supply
  the throw outside the design.
- **The fingerprint:** under center and in motion, 21 or heavy personnel (49ers), play-action at the top of the
  league (Rams), and receivers who gain far more after the catch than the catch predicts. From 2019 to 2025 the
  49ers were first in YAC over expected by a wide margin and top ten in EPA per play in six of seven seasons.
- **Label every staff by season.** In 2025 the family called plays in San Francisco, Los Angeles, Green Bay, Miami and
  Seattle (Super Bowl LX champions); in 2026, Kubiak and Mike LaFleur are head coaches in Las Vegas and Arizona,
  McDaniel is the Chargers' coordinator and Fleury calls Seattle's plays.
